title: Knowing our numbers
subject: Mathematics
summary: Large numbers are read, written and compared using place value and rounding.
points: The Indian system groups digits as ones, thousands, lakhs and crores.
The international system groups in thousands, millions and billions.
Comparing numbers starts with the number of digits, then the leftmost digit.
Rounding to the nearest ten, hundred or thousand makes estimation easier.

formulas.name: Indian place values
formulas.expr: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, lakh, ten lakh, crore

example: 7,45,32,891 is read as seven crore forty-five lakh thirty-two thousand eight hundred ninety-one.
mistakes: Mixing the Indian and international grouping.
Rounding before comparing numbers.

title: Whole numbers
subject: Mathematics
summary: Whole numbers start at 0, and their properties such as commutativity and distributivity simplify calculations.
points: Natural numbers start at 1; whole numbers include 0.
Addition and multiplication are commutative and associative; subtraction and division are not.
The distributive property links multiplication with addition and subtraction.
The number line shows order and helps with addition and subtraction.

formulas.name: Distributive
formulas.expr: a × (b + c) = a × b + a × c

example: 25 × 12 = 25 × (10 + 2) = 250 + 50 = 300 using distributivity.
mistakes: Assuming subtraction is commutative.
Forgetting that 0 is a whole number but not a natural number.

title: Playing with numbers
subject: Mathematics
summary: Divisibility rules, factors, multiples, HCF and LCM help solve number problems quickly.
points: A number is divisible by 3 if its digit sum is divisible by 3, by 9 if the digit sum is divisible by 9.
Divisibility by 4 depends on the last two digits; by 8 on the last three.
Every number can be written as a product of primes.
HCF is the largest common factor and LCM the smallest common multiple.
For two numbers, HCF × LCM = product of the numbers.

formulas.name: HCF–LCM relation
formulas.expr: HCF(a, b) × LCM(a, b) = a × b

example: HCF of 12 and 18 is 6, so LCM = 216/6 = 36.
mistakes: Using the HCF–LCM relation for more than two numbers.
Checking divisibility by 6 using only 2 or only 3.

title: Squares, cubes and their roots
subject: Mathematics
summary: A square is a number multiplied by itself, and a square root reverses that; cubes work the same way with three factors.
points: Perfect squares end in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9, never 2, 3, 7 or 8.
A square root can be found by prime factorisation or long division.
A perfect cube's prime factors appear in groups of three.
The cube root of a negative number is negative.
mistakes: Assuming every number has a whole-number square root.
Forgetting the negative root when solving x² = 9.

title: Direct and inverse proportion
subject: Mathematics
summary: In direct proportion both quantities increase together; in inverse proportion one falls as the other rises.
points: Direct proportion means the ratio x/y is constant.
Inverse proportion means the product x × y is constant.
Unitary method solves proportion problems by finding the value of one unit.
Time and workers, or speed and time for fixed distance, are inverse relationships.
example: If 4 workers take 6 days, 8 workers take 3 days — inverse proportion.
mistakes: Treating an inverse relationship as direct.
Forgetting to keep units consistent.

title: Introduction to graphs
subject: Mathematics
summary: Graphs show relationships between two quantities using axes, coordinates and lines.
points: A bar graph compares categories; a line graph shows change over time.
A pie chart shows parts of a whole.
A linear graph is a straight line and shows a constant rate.
The coordinates of a point are read as (x, y).

formulas.name: Linear graph
formulas.expr: y = mx + c has slope m and intercept c

example: A distance–time graph with a straight sloping line means constant speed.
mistakes: Joining bar-graph tops with a line when the data are categories.
Reading axes in the wrong order.

title: Symmetry and visualising solid shapes
subject: Mathematics
summary: Symmetry describes balanced shapes, and solids can be viewed as top, front and side views or flattened into nets.
points: A line of symmetry divides a figure into two mirror halves.
Regular polygons have as many lines of symmetry as sides.
Rotational symmetry concerns turns that leave a figure looking the same.
A net is a flat pattern that folds into a solid.
Solids have faces, edges and vertices; Euler's relation connects them.
example: A cube has 6 faces, 8 vertices and 12 edges, and 6 + 8 − 12 = 2.
mistakes: Counting diagonal lines as lines of symmetry for a rectangle.
Confusing edges and faces.

title: Food: where does it come from?
subject: Science
summary: Food comes from plants and animals, and different parts of plants are eaten.
points: Plant foods include roots, stems, leaves, flowers, fruits and seeds.
Animal foods include milk, eggs, meat and honey.
Some animals are herbivores, some carnivores and some omnivores.
Sprouted seeds and a balanced diet improve nutrition.
example: Carrot is a root, spinach is a leaf and rice is a seed.
aliases: food where does it come from
mistakes: Calling potato a root; it is a modified stem.
Assuming all plant parts are edible.

title: Components of food
subject: Science
summary: Food contains carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water, each with a specific role.
points: Carbohydrates and fats give energy; proteins build and repair the body.
Vitamins and minerals protect against disease and are needed in small amounts.
Roughage aids digestion and water regulates body processes.
Deficiency diseases include scurvy (vitamin C) and beriberi (vitamin B1).
A balanced diet supplies all nutrients in the right amounts.
example: A child with bleeding gums may lack vitamin C, causing scurvy.
mistakes: Thinking fats are always harmful.
Ignoring fibre in the diet.

title: Fibre to fabric
subject: Science
summary: Cloth comes from natural fibres such as cotton, jute, silk and wool, or synthetic fibres, through spinning and weaving.
points: Cotton and jute are plant fibres; silk and wool are animal fibres.
Ginning separates cotton fibres from seeds; spinning twists fibres into yarn.
Weaving and knitting turn yarn into fabric.
Sericulture is silk production and sheep rearing gives wool.
Synthetic fibres such as nylon and polyester are made from chemicals.
example: Cotton bolls are picked, ginned, spun into yarn and woven into cloth.
mistakes: Calling silk a plant fibre.
Confusing spinning with weaving.

title: Sorting materials into groups
subject: Science
summary: Materials are grouped by properties such as appearance, hardness, solubility, transparency and conductivity.
points: Materials may be lustrous or dull, hard or soft, opaque, translucent or transparent.
Some materials dissolve in water and others do not.
Metals generally conduct heat and electricity; most non-metals do not.
Objects may be made of one material or a combination chosen for its properties.
example: A cooking pan has a metal body for conduction and a plastic handle to insulate.
mistakes: Assuming all shiny materials are metals.
Confusing translucent with transparent.

title: Getting to know plants
subject: Science
summary: Plants have roots, stems, leaves, flowers and fruits, each with a function.
points: Roots absorb water and minerals and anchor the plant.
Stems support leaves and transport water and food.
Leaves make food by photosynthesis and exchange gases through stomata.
Flowers are reproductive parts; fruits protect seeds.
Plants may be herbs, shrubs or trees.
example: Water travels from roots through the stem to the leaves in the xylem.
mistakes: Thinking leaves only make food and do not lose water.
Calling all small plants herbs.

title: Body movements
subject: Science
summary: Animals move using bones, joints and muscles, and the human skeleton supports and protects the body.
points: The skeleton has the skull, backbone, rib cage, limbs and girdles.
Joints may be ball and socket, hinge, pivot or fixed.
Muscles pull on bones to produce movement and work in pairs.
Earthworms move by contracting body muscles against the ground.
Snails and snakes move without limbs using muscular waves.
example: The elbow is a hinge joint that allows movement in one plane.
mistakes: Saying muscles push bones.
Confusing a hinge joint with a ball and socket joint.

title: Light, shadows and reflections
subject: Science
summary: Light travels in straight lines, and objects block it to form shadows or reflect it into our eyes.
points: Transparent objects let light pass; opaque objects block it; translucent objects let some light through.
A shadow forms behind an opaque object and needs a screen.
Shadows are dark because light cannot bend around the object.
Mirrors reflect light and can form images.
A pinhole camera forms an inverted image because light travels in straight lines.
example: A pinhole camera image is upside down because rays cross at the hole.
mistakes: Thinking shadows need no light source behind the object.
Believing light bends around corners.

title: Electric circuits
subject: Science
summary: A circuit is a closed path through which electric current flows, and a switch controls it.
points: A cell has two terminals and drives current through a closed circuit.
A bulb glows when current passes through its filament.
An open circuit stops current; a switch opens or closes the path.
Series circuits share one path; parallel circuits have separate branches.
Conductors allow current, insulators resist it.
example: If one bulb in a series circuit fails, the whole circuit goes dark.
mistakes: Thinking current is used up as it flows.
Assuming a bulb glows with one wire connected.

title: Weather, climate and adaptations
subject: Science
summary: Weather is the day-to-day state of the atmosphere, and climate is the average pattern over years; animals adapt to both.
points: Weather changes quickly; climate changes over long periods.
Polar animals have thick fur and blubber; desert animals conserve water.
Tropical rainforest animals have adaptations for climbing and heavy rain.
Migration and hibernation are behavioural adaptations.
Adaptations help animals survive extremes of temperature and moisture.
example: A polar bear's white fur camouflages it and its blubber insulates it from cold.
mistakes: Using weather and climate interchangeably.
Assuming adaptation happens within one lifetime.

title: Winds, storms and cyclones
subject: Science
summary: Air moves from high to low pressure, and this movement produces winds, storms and cyclones.
points: Moving air is wind; it is caused by uneven heating of the earth.
A cyclone forms over warm oceans with low pressure at the centre and high-speed rotating winds.
Thunderstorms bring lightning, thunder and heavy rain.
The eye of a cyclone is calm while the surrounding wall has the strongest winds.
Safety steps include listening to warnings and staying indoors.
example: Warm sea water evaporates, rises, and the surrounding air rushes in, starting a cyclone.
mistakes: Thinking the eye is the most dangerous part.
Ignoring the need for early warnings.

title: Electric current and its effects
subject: Science
summary: Electric current produces heating, magnetic and chemical effects that are used in everyday devices.
points: A wire heats up when current flows through it, which is used in heaters and fuses.
A current-carrying coil behaves as an electromagnet.
An electric bell uses an electromagnet to strike a gong.
Fuses and circuit breakers protect circuits from excess current.
Electromagnets are used in cranes, motors and loudspeakers.
example: A fuse wire melts and breaks the circuit when current becomes too high.
mistakes: Thinking a fuse protects against voltage only.
Assuming electromagnets work without current.

title: Chemical effects of electric current
subject: Science
summary: Passing current through a conducting liquid causes chemical changes at the electrodes, a process called electrolysis.
points: Electrolytes are liquids or solutions that conduct electricity through ions.
Electrolysis decomposes a compound at the electrodes.
Electroplating deposits a thin metal layer for appearance or protection.
Some liquids conduct very weakly, so a tester or LED may not glow brightly.
Electrodes may be inert or reactive and affect the products.
example: A copper spoon electroplated with silver looks shiny and resists corrosion.
mistakes: Thinking all liquids conduct electricity.
Confusing electrolysis with a simple circuit.

title: Some natural phenomena
subject: Science
summary: Lightning and earthquakes show the power of electric charge and moving tectonic plates.
points: Lightning is caused by the build-up of static charge in clouds.
A lightning conductor safely carries charge to the ground.
Earthquakes occur when rocks along faults suddenly move.
Seismographs record earthquake magnitude on the Richter scale.
Safety during an earthquake means dropping, covering and holding under a strong table.

formulas.name: Richter scale
formulas.expr: logarithmic: each unit is about 10 times the amplitude

example: A metal rod fixed on a building protects it by conducting lightning to the earth.
mistakes: Thinking earthquakes can be predicted exactly.
Standing under a tree during lightning.

title: Stars and the solar system
subject: Science
summary: The solar system has the sun, eight planets, moons and smaller bodies, and stars are distant suns.
points: Planets in order are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.
The moon reflects sunlight and shows phases through the month.
Asteroids lie between Mars and Jupiter; comets have bright tails.
Light from the sun takes about 8 minutes to reach the earth.
Constellations are patterns of stars such as Ursa Major and Orion.
example: Pluto is classified as a dwarf planet, not one of the eight planets.
mistakes: Calling Pluto a planet.
Thinking the moon produces its own light.

title: Synthetic fibres and plastics
subject: Science
summary: Synthetic fibres and plastics are made from petrochemicals and have useful properties but environmental costs.
points: Rayon, nylon, polyester and acrylic are common synthetic fibres.
Synthetic fibres are strong, quick-drying and cheap but do not absorb water well.
Thermoplastics soften on heating; thermosetting plastics do not.
Plastics are light and durable but non-biodegradable.
Reducing single-use plastic and recycling lessen the damage.
example: Melamine is a thermosetting plastic used in unbreakable crockery.
mistakes: Thinking all plastics can be melted and remoulded.
Calling synthetic fibres eco-friendly.

title: Reaching the age of adolescence
subject: Science
summary: Adolescence is the transition from childhood to adulthood, marked by growth spurt, hormonal changes and puberty.
points: Puberty begins when the pituitary gland stimulates sex glands.
Secondary sexual characters develop during adolescence.
Hormones regulate growth, reproduction and metabolism.
Nutrition, hygiene and rest matter during rapid growth.
Adolescents need accurate information and emotional support.
example: A growth spurt in height is an early sign of puberty in both boys and girls.
mistakes: Treating adolescence as only physical change.
Ignoring the role of the pituitary gland.

title: From the earliest people to early cities
subject: History
summary: Early humans hunted, gathered and later farmed, and advances in tools, fire and agriculture shaped their lives.
points: Hunter-gatherers used stone tools and moved with seasons and animal herds.
Rock paintings at Bhimbetka show early human life.
Farming and animal domestication began in the Neolithic period.
Settled agriculture led to villages, pottery and storage.
Sources include archaeology, tools, bones and cave paintings.
example: Grain storage pits at early villages show surplus farming.
mistakes: Calling all early humans farmers.
Ignoring archaeology as a source.

title: Vital villages, thriving towns
subject: History
summary: From about 1000 BCE, iron tools, irrigation and trade supported villages and towns in the Indian subcontinent.
points: Iron ploughshares and irrigation increased farm yields.
Villages used tanks and canals to store and supply water.
Mathura became a major settlement and trade centre.
Crafts and long-distance trade linked towns to villages.
Assemblies and chiefs governed early settlements.
example: Mathura's location on trade routes helped it grow as a city.
mistakes: Assuming towns grew without agricultural surplus.
Ignoring the role of iron tools.

title: Traders, kings and pilgrims
subject: History
summary: Trade, religious travel and dynastic ambition connected India with Central Asia, the Mediterranean and Southeast Asia.
points: South India traded spices, textiles and gems with the Roman empire.
Muziris and Arikamedu were important port sites.
The Silk Route linked India to China and Central Asia.
Buddhist pilgrims travelled to sacred sites and left accounts.
Trade brought gold, wine and new ideas into India.
example: Roman coins found in south India show long-distance trade.
mistakes: Thinking trade was only within India.
Ignoring the role of pilgrims as travellers.

title: Regional cultures and religious developments
subject: History
summary: Between the eighth and eighteenth centuries, regional cultures and Bhakti–Sufi movements shaped Indian society.
points: Bhakti saints such as Kabir, Mirabai and Tukaram composed in local languages.
Sufi shrines became centres of devotion and community.
Regional cultures developed distinct architecture, language and festivals.
Manuscripts, paintings and music preserved these traditions.
Movements often challenged caste and ritual hierarchy.
example: Kabir's verses criticised both ritualism and sectarianism in simple language.
mistakes: Treating Bhakti and Sufi movements as identical.
Ignoring regional languages.

title: Eighteenth-century political formations
subject: History
summary: After the Mughal decline, regional states such as the Marathas, Sikhs, Rajputs and Jats emerged as powerful political centres.
points: Mughal authority weakened after Aurangzeb, with costly wars and succession disputes.
The Marathas built a large confederacy under Shivaji and the Peshwas.
The Sikhs consolidated under Guru Gobind Singh and later Ranjit Singh.
Nawabs, Rajputs and Jats ruled regional kingdoms.
The eighteenth century was not simply chaotic; it saw vibrant regional economies.
example: The Maratha confederacy expanded across central and northern India in the eighteenth century.
mistakes: Calling the eighteenth century a dark age.
Assuming the Mughals vanished immediately.

title: Tribals, dikus and the vision of a golden age
subject: History
summary: Colonial forest and revenue policies disrupted tribal economies and provoked movements such as Birsa Munda's.
points: Tribal groups practised shifting cultivation, hunting and gathering.
Moneylenders and traders (dikus) took land and produce through debt.
Forest laws restricted access to customary resources.
Birsa Munda led the Munda rebellion in Chhotanagpur against land alienation.
Tribal movements combined livelihood demands with cultural identity.
example: The Chhotanagpur Tenancy Act followed the Munda rebellion and restricted land transfer.
mistakes: Treating tribal society as unchanging.
Ignoring the role of moneylenders.

title: Women, caste and reform
subject: History
summary: Social reformers debated sati, widow remarriage, education for girls and caste inequality in the nineteenth century.
points: Raja Rammohan Roy campaigned against sati.
Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar promoted widow remarriage.
Jyotirao Phule and B. R. Ambedkar challenged caste hierarchy.
Women reformers such as Pandita Ramabai and Tarabai Shinde wrote and organised.
Reform was contested, and laws changed gradually.
example: The Widow Remarriage Act 1856 legalised remarriage for Hindu widows.
mistakes: Assuming reform was universally welcomed.
Crediting only male reformers.

title: The making of the national movement 1870s–1947
subject: History
summary: Indian nationalism grew from early associations through the Congress, mass movements and finally independence.
points: The Indian National Congress was founded in 1885.
Moderates demanded reform; radicals such as Tilak demanded swaraj.
Gandhi's non-cooperation, civil disobedience and quit India movements mobilised millions.
Muslim League, Hindu Mahasabha and other organisations shaped communal politics.
Independence in 1947 came with partition.
example: The Dandi march of 1930 began civil disobedience against the salt tax.
mistakes: Treating the freedom struggle as a single event.
Ignoring divisions within the movement.

title: India after independence
subject: History
summary: Independent India faced partition, integration of states, constitution making and planned development.
points: Partition displaced millions and created India and Pakistan.
Princely states were integrated through negotiation and accession.
The Constitution came into force in 1950 with universal adult franchise.
Linguistic states were reorganised in 1956.
Five Year Plans aimed at industrial and agricultural growth.
example: The States Reorganisation Act 1956 created states based mainly on language.
mistakes: Assuming integration was peaceful everywhere.
Ignoring the human cost of partition.

title: Our environment: natural and human
subject: Geography
summary: The environment includes natural surroundings and human-made systems, and people modify nature to meet needs.
points: The natural environment has land, water, air, plants and animals.
The human environment includes settlements, agriculture, industry and transport.
Human activity changes the environment and can damage it.
Sustainable practices balance human needs with environmental limits.
example: Cutting hills for roads changes drainage and can cause landslides.
mistakes: Treating the environment as only nature.
Ignoring human-made environments.

title: Inside our earth
subject: Geography
summary: The earth has layers — crust, mantle and core — and rocks are of three main types.
points: The crust is the thin outer layer; the mantle lies below it; the core is at the centre.
Igneous rocks form from cooling magma, sedimentary from deposition, metamorphic from heat and pressure.
The rock cycle converts one rock type into another over time.
Minerals are the building blocks of rocks.
example: Granite is an igneous rock that cooled slowly underground.
mistakes: Thinking the crust is the thickest layer.
Assuming rocks never change type.

title: Our changing earth
subject: Geography
summary: Endogenic forces build landforms and exogenic forces such as water, wind and ice wear them down.
points: Earthquakes and volcanoes are endogenic processes.
Rivers erode valleys, form meanders and deposit floodplains and deltas.
Glaciers carve U-shaped valleys and deposit moraines.
Wind forms dunes and mushroom rocks in deserts.
Sea waves cut cliffs and build beaches.
example: The Grand Canyon was carved by river erosion over millions of years.
mistakes: Assuming landforms form quickly.
Confusing erosion with deposition.

title: Air and water
subject: Geography
summary: Air and water are renewable resources whose quality and availability depend on natural cycles and human use.
points: Air is a mixture of gases; the atmosphere has five layers.
Weather and climate are shaped by temperature, pressure, wind and moisture.
Water covers about three-fourths of the earth's surface but fresh water is scarce.
The water cycle renews fresh water through evaporation and precipitation.
Pollution and overuse threaten both resources.
example: Groundwater depletion lowers the water table and dries wells.
mistakes: Assuming fresh water is abundant.
Treating air as a single gas.

title: Human environment: settlements and transport
subject: Geography
summary: People live in rural and urban settlements linked by transport and communication.
points: Rural settlements are villages; urban settlements are towns and cities.
Compact and dispersed patterns depend on terrain, water and land.
Transport modes include road, rail, water and air.
Communication links people through post, telephone and internet.
Cities offer services but face congestion and pollution.
example: A hill village may have dispersed houses because flat land is scarce.
mistakes: Assuming all villages look alike.
Ignoring transport in settlement growth.

title: Resources
subject: Geography
summary: Resources are things people use from nature; they are classified by utility, exhaustibility and ownership.
points: Natural resources include land, water, forests, minerals and energy.
Renewable resources can be replenished; non-renewable cannot.
Resources may be individual, community, national or international.
Human resources are people's skills and abilities.
Conservation means using resources wisely for the future.
example: Community resources include village ponds and grazing land.
mistakes: Classifying coal as renewable.
Ignoring human resources.

title: Mineral and power resources
subject: Geography
summary: Minerals and energy resources are unevenly distributed and must be conserved.
points: Minerals may be metallic (iron, copper) or non-metallic (limestone, mica).
Mining can be open-cast, shaft or drilling based.
Conventional energy sources include coal, petroleum, natural gas and hydro.
Non-conventional sources include solar, wind, tidal, geothermal and biogas.
Conservation reduces waste and extends resource life.
example: Iron ore is a metallic mineral used to make steel.
mistakes: Confusing minerals with rocks.
Treating fossil fuels as renewable.

title: Industries
subject: Geography
summary: Industries process raw materials into goods and are classified by size, ownership and inputs.
points: Industries may be primary, secondary or tertiary.
Classification by size: cottage, small scale, large scale.
Classification by ownership: private, public, joint and cooperative.
Location depends on raw materials, power, transport, labour and market.
Industries cause pollution and need cleaner technology.
example: A steel plant is located near iron ore, coal and transport routes.
mistakes: Assuming all industries are large factories.
Ignoring transport in location decisions.

title: Human resources
subject: Geography
summary: People are a resource whose value depends on health, education and skills.
points: Population becomes human capital through education and health.
Population density and distribution vary widely.
Literacy and skill levels affect productivity.
Migration changes the distribution of human resources.
Investing in people raises national development.
example: A country with high literacy tends to have more skilled workers.
mistakes: Equating a large population with developed human resources.
Ignoring health in human capital.

title: Diversity and discrimination
subject: Civics
summary: India is diverse in language, religion and culture, and discrimination denies equality to some groups.
points: Diversity enriches society but can also be a source of prejudice.
Discrimination occurs on the basis of caste, religion, gender and region.
The Constitution guarantees equality and prohibits discrimination.
Prejudice is an attitude; discrimination is behaviour.
Recognising stereotypes is the first step to challenging them.
example: Refusing to rent a house to someone because of religion is discrimination.
mistakes: Confusing prejudice with discrimination.
Assuming diversity causes conflict necessarily.

title: What is government?
subject: Civics
summary: Government makes decisions, implements them and provides services for a country or region.
points: Governments make laws, run services and manage resources.
Levels include local, state and national.
In a democracy people choose representatives through elections.
Governments are accountable to citizens and the courts.
Universal adult franchise gives every adult a vote.
example: A municipal corporation maintains roads and garbage collection in a city.
mistakes: Thinking government means only the central government.
Ignoring local government.

title: Equality in Indian democracy
subject: Civics
summary: Equality means all citizens have the same rights and dignity, and the state acts against discrimination.
points: The Constitution guarantees equality before the law.
Untouchability is abolished and its practice is an offence.
Affirmative action helps disadvantaged groups access education and jobs.
Inequality persists in wages, access and social treatment.
Courts and commissions enforce equality rights.
example: Reservation in educational institutions is a measure to address historical inequality.
mistakes: Thinking equality means treating everyone identically in every situation.
Assuming discrimination has ended.

title: State government
subject: Civics
summary: Each state has a legislature, a chief minister and a governor, with powers divided from the centre.
points: The Governor is the constitutional head of the state; the Chief Minister heads the government.
The state legislature may be unicameral or bicameral.
State governments handle police, health, education and agriculture.
The Legislative Assembly is directly elected by voters.
The centre and states share certain subjects under the Constitution.
example: A state assembly passes laws on local schools and hospitals.
mistakes: Thinking the Governor makes policy independently.
Confusing the Assembly with the Council.

title: Media and markets
subject: Civics
summary: Media informs and shapes opinion, while markets connect buyers and sellers with different kinds of shops and prices.
points: Media includes newspapers, television, radio and the internet.
Media should be independent and factual; advertising can bias content.
Markets range from weekly haats to malls and online platforms.
Prices vary with place, quality and bargaining.
Consumers have rights and should compare and check quality.
example: A weekly haat sells local produce directly from farmers to buyers.
mistakes: Treating all media information as neutral.
Assuming the cheapest price is always best value.

title: The Indian Constitution and the rule of law
subject: Civics
summary: The Constitution is the supreme law that sets out rights, duties and the structure of government.
points: It defines the powers of the legislature, executive and judiciary.
Fundamental rights protect citizens; fundamental duties remind them of obligations.
The rule of law means no one is above the law.
The Constitution can be amended but its basic structure is protected.
It applies to all persons in India, with some rights only for citizens.
example: A law that violates fundamental rights can be struck down by the courts.
mistakes: Thinking the Constitution is only for lawyers.
Ignoring fundamental duties.

title: Understanding secularism
subject: Civics
summary: Indian secularism means the state does not favour any religion and treats all religions with equal respect.
points: The state has no official religion.
It can intervene to reform practices that violate rights, such as untouchability.
It may support religious minorities to promote equality.
Freedom of religion is a fundamental right.
Secularism protects both believers and non-believers.
example: The state funds schools for all communities without teaching one religion as superior.
mistakes: Equating secularism with hostility to religion.
Assuming all countries define secularism the same way.

title: Marginalisation and social justice
subject: Civics
summary: Some groups face exclusion from resources and opportunities, and the Constitution provides safeguards.
points: Adivasis, Dalits, minorities and women have faced historical exclusion.
Reservation, protective laws and welfare schemes address disadvantage.
Marginalisation can be economic, social or political.
Access to land, education and justice is central to inclusion.
Agencies such as the SC/ST Commission monitor safeguards.
example: The Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act protects against caste violence.
mistakes: Treating marginalisation as only economic.
Assuming legal protection ends discrimination.

title: Public facilities
subject: Civics
summary: Public facilities such as water, sanitation, health care and schools are essential and often provided by government.
points: Water, electricity, sanitation and public transport are basic facilities.
Markets alone may not provide them to everyone at an affordable price.
The government funds them through taxes.
Their quality affects health, education and dignity.
Citizens can demand accountability for service delivery.
example: A safe drinking water supply reduces waterborne disease in a locality.
mistakes: Assuming private markets serve everyone equally.
Ignoring the link between facilities and health.

title: Law and social justice
subject: Civics
summary: Laws protect workers, consumers and the environment, and courts enforce them.
points: Labour laws set minimum wages, safety and working hours.
The Bhopal gas tragedy led to stronger environmental and compensation laws.
Consumer protection law gives redress for defective goods and services.
Enforcement depends on inspection, courts and public awareness.
Weak enforcement allows exploitation to continue.
example: The Bhopal gas leak in 1984 prompted the Environment Protection Act 1986.
mistakes: Thinking a law is effective as soon as it is passed.
Ignoring enforcement problems.

title: Reading literature: prose, poetry and drama
subject: English
summary: Literature is studied through theme, character, plot, setting, tone and poetic devices rather than plot summary alone.
points: Theme is the central idea; it must be supported with evidence from the text.
Character analysis uses actions, speech and others' reactions.
Poetry analysis examines form, rhyme, imagery, tone and figures of speech.
Drama adds stage directions, dialogue and dramatic irony.
Answers should quote briefly and explain, not just retell the story.
example: A poem's repeated image of darkness may build a tone of loss rather than simply describe night.
mistakes: Retelling the plot instead of analysing.
Naming a device without explaining its effect.
